game-rules/paths/tugging-at-heartstrings.title: Tugging at Heartstrings
game-rules/paths/tugging-at-heartstrings.content:
Tugging at Heartstrings
flowchart TD
	id["Starting abilities"] --> Example1
	id["Starting abilities"] --> Example2

Starting Abilities
Heartstring clock. Every character has a heartstring clock. It starts empty, and character level number of segments. Once a heartstring clock is filled, the character gains 1 heartstring level and clock resets.
Heartstring Level. The measure of how much controll you gained over a character. A level is gained by filling out a heartstring clock.
Hearstrings. Heartstring is a sentence or phrase, that describes important traits, bonds, motivations and other character features. Every character has at least one  heartstring.
Marionette.  Any time an ability other then Tug at the heartstrings is used, a marionette handle and strings manifest above the target for the duration of the ability. There are heartstring level number of strings connecting the handle to the target. If the strings is cut, the targets heartstring level is reduced by that number.


                  
                  How does marionette work with instant abilities?
                  
                

It’s possible to cut strings even when used with these kinds of abilities. For example, when using String along, someone can try to attack while the target is being pulled. During action scenes, this would mean taking such action on the same round.


Marionette Strings. Each string can take at most 1 minor wound. Defending is treated as a roll performed by you. You are skilled in this roll.


                  
                  Tug at the heartstrings 
                  
                


Free Action/Action, cost(1 Might)

Talk to someone, and attempt to move their hearts. To do this, you must be able communicate with the target, and the topic must be one of their heartstrings. On success, fill one segment of their Heatstring clock.
Verbal communication is a Free Action. When communication requires more effort then just speaking, such as writing or dance, the ability requires Action.
Self-Amp: For every amp, you can cover additional target.
Amp: For every 2 successes, tick additional clock.




                  
                  Follow your heart! 
                  
                


Free Action, cost(1 Soul, 1+ Heartstring level)

Consume some of the targets current heartstring level, formulate a goal, and determine your endorsement/dissaproval of the chosen goal. Whenever the target takes an action toward accomplishing the goal, it’s easer (endorsement) or hindered (disaproval) by the consumed heartstring level.
Self-Amp: For every amp, you can cover additional target. The targets must all share same goal and endorsement/dissaproval.




                  
                  String along 
                  
                


Free Action, cost(1 Soul), heartstring level at least 1

Pull your target in a chosen direction by 5 meters.
Amp: Move the target additional 5 meters per amp. Every 3rd amp adds aditional 5 meters.




                  
                  Student of the heart 
                  
                

You gain a skill: Discerning motivations

game-rules/playing-the-game/amp.title: Amp
game-rules/playing-the-game/amp.content:
Amp
Some abilities gain stronger effects with more successes on a roll. This mechanic is call Amp(lificatio).  When rolling, all extra successes above the 1st are called Amps. If your roll succeeded 3 times, you have 2 Amps. You will find what the bonuses gained are in the description of the ability in the paragraph starting with Amp:.
The the bonus will grow with each Amp. Most of them will fall into one of these types:

Deal extra (minor) wound for each Amp. Sometimes, every Nth Amp will deal major wound.
The effect grows in area or scope for each Amp (more targets, greater area or range, etc.). Sometimes, every Nth Amp will be a greater bonus.
Choose one bonus effect from the list of options. Every extra Amp means 1 extra effect.

Self-Amp
This is a special kind of Amp that comes with it’s own Difficulty. You can view this as a roll to determine how well you execute the action.
When using the ability with Self-Amp, you can make a roll against its difficulty. Failure means you only get the base effect. Success means you get extra bonuses. Unlike regular Amp, all successes count as Self-Amp.


                  
                  Example
                  
                

You take an action to try and throw tree at your enemy, using an ability that grants you superhuman strength.
This ability has a Self-Amp that increases the weight and size of an object you can lift and throw. For each Self-Amp the weight is double yours, and you require 3 Self-Amp to throw it. To hit your enemy, you have to roll Diff 4. The Self-Amp is Diff 5.
You roll 5d6, ending up with (5,6, 4, 2, 1). You rolled enough to be able to hit the enemy, but you only got 2 Self-Amp. You fail to lift the tree, and therefore fail the action to attack




                  
                  Tip
                  
                

Self-Amps are awlays a Diff 5 roll using the pool associated with that ability. The bonuses are described in paragraphs starting with Self-Amp:.

game-rules/playing-the-game/rolling-dice.title: Rolling dice
game-rules/playing-the-game/rolling-dice.content:
Rolling dice
Whenever an action asks for a roll, you go through the following steps:

Determine the roll difficulty. This will always be a number between 1 and 12. It’s determined by the GM, or written as part of the ability description. A single roll can have multiple difficulties.



                  
                  Example
                  
                

You are rolling Diff 3 (Body) to climb up a tree. The difficulty of the roll is 3.



Determine if you are skilled in the action. If an action benefits from your skill, you add your Skill die to the roll.



                  
                  Example
                  
                

Your character is skilled at climbing, you get to add your a d6 (your Skill die) to your roll.



Assemble the dice you will roll. Expend dice from your Might, Body, Soul, and Drive die pools, and add them to this roll. You can expend at most 15 dice. A single roll can use at most 16 dice; 15 from the pool and 1 Skill Die.



                  
                  Example
                  
                

You expend 2d6 from your Might pool and 1d6 from your Body pool. Your entire roll will therefore be 4d6, including the Skill die.



Roll the dice. Roll all the dice, and apply any roll modifiers. Even if the role has multiple difficulties or multiple targets, you only make one roll. You roll 4d6, and get: 2, 3, 1, 6.
Determine if roll succeeded. When any of the dice rolls on a number equal to or above the difficulty, it counts as a success. If you have at least one successful roll, the entire roll is success. In rolls with multiple difficulties, you have do this for every difficulty.



                  
                  Example
                  
                

The difficulty of the roll was 3, therefore you have 2 successes (rolls 3 and 6). Since you have at least 1 success, the entire roll is successful.



Determine the Amp. Every success die above the first is considered an amp(lification) die, improving your outcome. Count all of the extra success you have, and check the description of your Action and Abilities you used to see if any of them have an Amp option.



                  
                  Example
                  
                

Your roll had 2 successes (rolls 3 and 6). That means you had 1 extra success above what you needed. This means you have 1 Amp.
You check your abilities, and find out you have an ability, that allows you to become familiar with anything you climb enough to automatically take someone up with you. The ability allows you to do guide number of people equal to your Amp.



Resolve the consequences. Tell the results of your roll, the Amp and its effects, to your GM. Together, you narrate the consequences of the roll.



                  
                  Example
                  
                

You manage to climb up the tree with ease. Thanks to your Amp, you grab one of your party members to go up with you. You both climb up all the way to the top of the tree, surveying the area.


Determining Difficulty
When choosing how difficult a task can be, you have to take into consideration that not all situations and characters are created equal. When hitting an opponent with an attack, setting a single difficulty for all players is a fairly simple concept. On the other hand, how to set a single difficulty in studying an advanced alchemical tome?
In other systems, this question might be answered by using single difficulty and roll modifiers. In our case, we differentiate between objective and subjective difficulty.


                  
                  Rough Guidelines 
                  
                

Difficulty 5. This difficulty is used for almost all Self-Amp rolls. It should relate to tasks where a regular person must apply their skills and experience to succeed.
Difficulty 6. This is the highest challenge a regular person might face. Backbreaking physical labor, and taxing mental tasks.
Difficulty 8. This difficulty should be one that requires an extremely talent person to succeed.
Difficulty 10. We are reaching difficulties face by very few people in history.
Difficulty 12. This difficulty would be reaching the limits of what is possible. In epic fantasy, these would be on par with Herculean tasks.


Objective difficulty
These almost always come into play when it comes to purely mechanical situations: attacks, defense, Self-amp, scene mechanics. These are usually the core mechanics to your play style, where you desire consistency and some degree of fairness.  As vague as this description might be, you will be fine with the following rule of thumb.


                  
                  Rule of thumb 
                  
                

Everything starts as objective difficulty, and might change into a subjective one after conversation between Player and the GM.


Subjective difficulty
Subjective difficulty is best defined by an example. The player sees group of villagers trying to lift up a stuck wagon. They decide they want to go over, and lift it up, and push it away. The first decision of the GM is to declare it a Diff 6 roll. The player then brings up an ability of theirs. It makes them far stronger then a regular person, allowing them to casually lift 1 ton, and to lift up to 2 tons. Taking this into account, the GM changes it to Diff 2, only to give some small chance to struggle.
Due to this improvised nature, there are no clear rules as to how to decide on a subjective ruling. Instead, best we can do is few guidelines:

If the characters natural predisposition should make a task easier, lower the difficulty.
If it makes the task trivial, make it automatic success or Diff 2. The Diff 2 gives a small chance of failure, that allows for a bit of variability.
When a character lacks predisposition to do something, consider making it an automatic failure. Understanding an advanced alchemical manual when a character barely knows what alchemy is impossible. Even a Diff 12 roll doesn’t change that.
When a character is bad at something as character feature, increase the difficulty. Some examples are physically weak, finds books boring, can’t see well.
When a character is temporarily held back or at an advantage, consider making the roll look at Using Hindered & Eased.

Using Hindered & Eased
While difficulty is about figuring out how hard it is to achieve the task on its own, the Hindered and Eased mechanics are about allowing temporary advantages to affect the roll. If a character is trying to catch up to someone by sprinting in the mud, their roll with be Hindered. Similarly, trying to outrun someone after leading them into a mud pit will make it Eased.


                  
                  Rule of Thumb 
                  
                

A single thing that helps or hold back should Ease or Hinder by 1. More severe one by 2. Extreme effect is 3.
You should avoid using larger numbers. These should be reserved for extreme, once in a game rare circumstances.




                  
                  Stacking Bonuses 
                  
                

Make use of stacking multiple bonuses. Each effect might ease or hinder by 1, eventually stacking up to an overall larger bonus. This will happen quite often in the game, due to player abilities.


                  
                  Stacking bonuses in combat 
                  
                
If a enemy is knocked prone and has sand thrown into their eyes, each of these would ease a player roll by 1, for total eased by 2 roll.



Additional rules
One action, one roll
Regardless of the number of targets or multiple difficulties, you only ever perform one roll. As such, an action only ever needs you to find one thing you are skilled at that applies, and to only ever expend dice from your pools once. Ability or a Boon also applies to the entire roll.
All dice can succeed
Whenever you make a roll, you may only roll the dice that can succeed. A difficulty 7 roll can only use d8 or larger. You can not include the d6 in the roll.
This become slightly more complex when it comes to multiple difficulties. In such cases the dice have to be able to succeed on at least one of the difficulties.


                  
                  Example
                  
                

You are rolling with Diff 6 and Diff 7. Your skill die is d6, and all your pools have only d6 dice. You can still continue with the roll, but you can only succeed on the Diff 6. The Diff 7 automatically fails.


Automatic failure
If you do not have any dice that can succeed on the difficulty of the roll, you automatically fail.


                  
                  Example
                  
                

You must succeed on a Diff 10 roll, but your skill die is d8, and the largest die in any of your pools is also d8. You are unable to succeed on this roll and automatically fail.




                  
                  Example
                  
                

You must succeed on a Diff 8 roll. You are not skilled in this Action, and therefore can not apply your skill die of d8. You expended all your d8 dice from Pools, and are only left with d6. You have no viable dice, and automatically fail on the roll.


Multiple difficulties
When a roll comes with multiple difficulties, you determine the success of each separately. You roll the dice once, and then count success for each Difficulty.


                  
                  Example
                  
                

You roll 4d6, Diff 6 to avoid being hit, and Diff 3 to be disarmed by the attack. You rolled 1, 4, 5, 5. You fail at the Diff 6, but you succeed on the Diff 3 (with 3 successes: 4, 5, 5).


In a scenario when your roll is Eased or Hindered it is important to consider the context of the roll. The roll modifiers should apply to only the dice that can succeed on the roll.


                  
                  Eased roll with multiple difficulties 
                  
                

You perform an action to cleave 2 enemies with your Axe. Only one of them is heavily armored and trained. Your friend decides to help you out with the stronger one, and uses an ability that Eases attacking them by 1.
Hitting the first one is Diff 5, while hitting the other is Diff 7 Eased by 1. You dice to go all in, and rolling 3d6+4d8. You roll (2, 3, 2) on the d6, and (5, 6, 2, 4) on the d8.
You can re-roll one failed die because the attack is eased. Since it was the Diff 7 attack that was Eased, you can only choose one of the d8 dice to re-roll.




                  
                  Eased roll with multiple difficulties, cont. 
                  
                

Lets change the previous example. This time, The Diff 5 roll is Eased by 1. Since all of the dice you used can succeed on the Diff 5, you can re-roll any d6 or d8 dice. You choose d8 and roll 7, succeeding on both attacks.




                  
                  Hindered roll with multiple difficulties 
                  
                

This time, your attack against armored enemy is hindered, and you manage to roll (2, 3, 2) on d6, and (8, 6, 2, 4) on d8. You must re-roll the one successful die. Since the the Diff 7 is the one Hindered, you must re-roll the only successful d8 roll. You end up rolling 5, and the both attacks fail.


Roll modifiers
The game uses two special modifiers: Eased and Hindered. Both of these allow you to re-roll dice during your roll. They share these rules:

Single die can only be re-rolled once.
If Eased or Hindered, you must re-roll if possible.
Eased and Hindered cancel each other out. If a roll is Eased by 2 and Hindered by 1, the roll will end up being Eased by 1.
If your roll is Eased by number larger then number of dice you rolled, miss out on extra re-roll. You can not re-roll same die twice.
If your roll is Hindered by number greater then number of dice you rolled, you avoid the extra re-rolls. You can not re-roll the same die twice.
You choose which of the dice gets re-rolled, as long as it is a die that can succeed on that difficulty.

Eased
Re-roll one of the failed dice in your roll.


                  
                  Example
                  
                

You are rolling Diff 6 Eased by 1. You rolled 3d6 for result of (2, 5, 3). You choose to re-roll the first die, rolling 6 and succeeding on the roll.


Hindered
Re-roll one of the success dice in your roll.


                  
                  Example
                  
                

You are rolling Diff 6 Hindered by 1. You rolled 3d8 for result of (2, 6, 7). You choose the second die, rolling 8 and succeeding on the roll with Amp 1s.


Multiple targets
If an action has more then one target, your roll will have a difficulty for each of the targets. The success will be resolved as a regular roll with multiple difficulties.

game-rules/playing-the-game/skills.title: Skills
game-rules/playing-the-game/skills.content:
Skills
Any time your character is supposed to be exceptionally good at something, they gain a skill in this thing. This mechanic is similar to proficiency in D&D and Pathfinder, skills in Cypher System, or skills in Draw Steel.
For the most part, there is no specific list of skills in this system. Instead, they are formulated with a single word, phrase, or sentence. For guidance on how to come up with a Skill, see Creating Skills.


                  
                  Skills 
                  
                


Climbing
Navigating Forests
Using Swords
Driving Vehicles
Carpentry
Creative writing
Learning & remembering surface level information



When taking an action, you should consult your list of skills. If any of the skills applies to the given action, you may use your skill die to the roll. Skill die does not count towards the 15 dice limit of a roll. You only add it to your roll once.


                  
                  Skill Die 
                  
                

Your skill die starts as d4 at level 1, and increases by size every odd numbered character level:

d4 at level 1
d6 at level 3
d8 at level 5
d10 at level 7
d12 at level 9





                  
                  Abilities & Skills 
                  
                

Your character is skilled at using an ability if it was gained from a perk.




                  
                  What if two skills apply to single roll? 
                  
                

You only add the skill die once, regardless of how many skills might apply to the action.




                  
                  Do i add skill die if it can not succeed on the roll? 
                  
                

No.
Even if you rolled, the Skill die can’t succeed on the roll because it is too small.


                  
                  Impossible difficulty 
                  
                
Your skill die is d6, but the roll is Diff 7. Unfortunately, you won’t be able to use the skill die, even when you are skilled at this action. You can still expend dice from your pool and attempt a roll.



                  
                  One of the multiple difficulties is impossible 
                  
                
The roll has two difficulties: Diff 5 and Diff 7. Your skill die is d6. You may roll the skill die. When resolving the action, your skill die only counts towards the Diff 5.





                  
                  Does skill die count towards ability cost? 
                  
                

No. Ability cost must be paid using dice from pools. Skill die is only used to give you an edge.


Creating Skills
We’ll split up creation process of an in-game skill into these steps:

Come up with a general description of the skill. This step is meant for both player and GM to have some idea. The two questions you want to answer is: What kind of actions does it apply to? How do you want to use it?
Adjust the scope based on your game.
Shorten the skill name.

Figuring out the scope
Not all skills are created equal. Imagine playing a game themed around typical dungeon fantasy. Character skilled in Using a sword, Fighting undead or Disabling traps gets to apply their skill generously. Meanwhile, a character with skill in Philosophy or Comparative Sociology will rarely get an option to do so.  This is the scope of the skill.
When creating a skill, you must take into account the type of game the character is used in. At the end of the day, this process will boil down to answering the question “How often do i get to use the skill for different actions?”:

Is it used for almost every (different) action? Make the scope of the skill smaller.
Do i rarely, or never, get to use the skill? Increase the scope of the skill.



                  
                  Is the scope always the reason why skill is overused/under-used? 
                  
                

Sometimes, skill doesn’t come into play for gameplay reasons. Skill in Disabling traps is a well-worded one, but might end up unused for several sessions if the dungeon has no traps. Skills don’t have to be used constantly and can always be revisited in the future. If it turns out that the skill becomes useless to a character, it’s time to revisit the skill.


                  
                  Changing skill 
                  
                
Changing the formulation of skill should always be combined effort of both the player and the GM.

On the other hand, some skills might be used too often because they are Core Skills to the game.


Formulating the scope of skills isn’t an exact science. Some skills will be central to the way the game is played, and could be considered Core Skills. For the rest, you can use the following advice:

Does the game revolve around using this skill? If so, you should consider making it smaller. Being skilled in Biology will have a different impact in a dungeon fantasy, then in a sci-fi fantasy where players investigate an abandoned research lab.
If the scope is too small, you can bundle multiple related skills together. Skill in Disabling traps might become Studying & manipulating mechanisms (locks, traps, etc.). Skill in recognizing edible mushrooms could become Foraging, poisonous flora.
If the scope is too small for areas of science or crafting, try searching for fields that encompass the one you want to be skilled it. Skill in Microbiology could become Biology.
When a skill’s scope is too large, look into specific fields with science or craftsmanship. If that won’t help, use the specific activity.

Core Skills
These skills usually come into play often and are integral to the gameplay. However, if you were to reduce their scope too much, the players will be forced into having only these Core Skills. In most games, these will be related to combat, persuasion, or lying.
When choosing skills, gaining Core Skills is usually more restricted and more desired by players. The general rule is, that if a player has an option to choose any Skill, they are not allowed to pick a Core Skill for your game.


                  
                  Epic Fantasy: Offense 
                  
                

In epic fantasy, you might choose between groups of weapons, types of weapons, or fighting styles.


                  
                  Fighting styles 
                  
                


Swordsmanship
Fencing
Dual wielding
Archery





                  
                  Weapons 
                  
                


Maces & Clubs
Spears
Bows
Axes





                  
                  Weapon types 
                  
                


Slashing weapons
Light weapons
Heavy Weapons
Oversized Weapons
Ranged weapons
You might also choose allow the combinations of each of these. This would be the recommended approach, as gives the players an option to express themselves.







                  
                  Epic Fantasy: Defense 
                  
                

While fighting, the character must be able to defend themselves. You have variety of options on how to implement this:


                  
                  Type of damage 
                  
                


Elemental
Mental
Physical
Decaying





                  
                  Type of attack / Source of damage 
                  
                


Magical
Weapon
Physical
Poisons
Disease
Natural





                  
                  Fighting styles 
                  
                


Swordsmanship
Fencing
Dual wielding
Archery
Magecraft



Once again, combination of these is the best solution. This way, a player can combine their play-style into a Core Skill, avoiding inflation of overly-granular skills. Character skilled in Fencing will be skilled at both attack and defense with their rapier, and still retain a weakness to defending against mental attacks.




                  
                  Attack & Defense in other formats 
                  
                

In games relying more on social scenes, the attack & defense can appear in other forms. While in a interacting a suspect, both parties are engaging in a form of verbal attack and defense. During a meeting of two factions, both sides are locked in a combat to try to convince, misdirect, lie to and see through the other side.


                  
                  Social "offensive" skills 
                  
                


Lying about self
Storytelling
Creating detailed stories
Attention to detail
Truthfulness
Empathy
Mirroring & Matching
Argumentative
Aggressiveness
Blackmailing
Faking Emotions





                  
                  Social "defensive" skills 
                  
                


Stubbornness
Verbal Analysis
Empathy
Attention to detail
Reading emotions
Observant
Following complicated threads of information
Surface level knowledge of topics
Easily remembering information

game-rules/playing-the-game/stat-pools.title: Stat Pools
game-rules/playing-the-game/stat-pools.content:
Stat pools
Your pools are the measure of how much can your character push themselves to achieve something. Each character has 4 pools, representing aspects and fueling actions in a slightly different way.
All pools besides Drive pool are fairly straightforward. They contain dice ranging from d6 to d12. Other then sizes, they are not split up in any other way. Each pool has it’s maximum size, that is the maximum number of dice of each size you can have. Pool can not increase the maximum in any other way besides leveling up your character. Once a pool is empty, you must restore dice before you can expend any dice from it.


                  
                  Short summary 
                  
                

Might pool. Represents power, stamina. You use and regain it often.
Body pool. Represents physical ability. Fuels physical abilities. Slow to regain.
Soul pool. Represents mental and supernatural ability. Fuels mental and supernatural abilities. Slow to regain.
Drive pool. Represents your motivation. You regain it a lot in situations that suit your character.




                  
                  Restoring a pool 
                  
                

This refers to regaining dice in your pool. Unless stated otherwise, it means rolling 1d4. You then regain that amount of expended dice in your pool.


                  
                  Lowest dice first. 
                  
                
When restoring a pool, you always regain the smallest expended dice first.
If your pool has 2/4 d6, and 2/4 d8, you should restore the d6’s first. You may only restore a d8 after you have regained all of the d6’s.





                  
                  Restoring pool & d4 
                  
                

The dice usually used in abilities allowing you to restore pools is d4. As a character grows stronger, they might gain modifiers to these rolls, or be allowed to roll multiple d4’s.


Might pool
Might is used to fuel all your abilities and act kind of like a stamina bar. You can treat it as an accumulation of all your mental and physical strength at your disposal. It is the most reliable source of dice, as every character has access to abilities for restoring Might pool.
Body & Soul pools
Body and Soul are a more limited resource. You restore dice in this pool by resting and longer recovery. As such, the dice in these pools are more valuable. The most common usage for them is ability cost, as some abilities require you to expend at least some dice from one of these pools.
When rolling, the GM or the ability will specify one either Body or Soul. You may only expend dice from one of these for this roll. Choosing which follows these guidelines:

Body is used for rolls and abilities relying on physical prowess. These can be anything from strength, speed to resistance.
Soul is used for rolls and abilities relying on mental and supernatural prowess. These can be anything from intelligence, memory, to magical affinity.

Drive pool
